Forgiveness is Not All About You

“Forgive and forget.”
“Just let go of the past.”
“Unforgiveness is holding someone prisoner and finding out that prisoner is you.”

Luke 6:28
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you.
Matthew 5:44
But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you,

Ephesians 4:31
 Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and evil speaking be put away from you, with all malice. 

The offense is meant to stop people’s destinies. If the enemy can get people to come against one another, to not have the best intentions toward one another, to not want the best for one another, then he can hinder us from stepping into all that God has for us and them. The fervent love we’re to have for one another is to earnestly want the best for each person, knowing they have a destiny in God and for His Kingdom. God knows how to correct out of love. That’s why vengeance is His. 
But nowhere in this forgiveness is there a provision to be a doormat. There’s nowhere where others are granted permission to steal from us. Using wisdom and recognizing a weakness in others neither banishes them to such a fate nor does it exempt them from having to show the fruits of repentance. Love keeps no record of wrongs (I Corinthians 13:5). It does so, not to allow ourselves to be trampled upon as a martyr, but to not seek or even desire retaliation. Love believes all things (I Corinthians 13:7). It never gives up believing that someone can break out of damaging patterns through the power of the Holy Spirit and walk into their callings and destinies. 
Can we stand to see our offenders prosper, to attain their heart’s desires? What’s more, can we hope for it in our hearts and without reservation? Doing so would require relinquishment of all bitterness, which can only be achieved if we trust God to not only correct them, but to flourish us. 


The reason vengeance belongs to God is because if we can’t let God administer it, then we want it for the wrong reasons. God always wants the best for the person and all vengeance will be from a place of love. It will be to correct but not destroy. It will be to use circumstances, both blessing and uncomfortable, to direct people towards their destiny. God knows how to do it right. We don’t have the vantage point to ever do it even close to right. 
Ultimately, forgiveness is an act of faith. It means that you trust that God doesn’t miss anything and that He cares about each and every thing you go through. It trusts Him to correct any slight against you, to restore, replenish, and refresh. It trusts Him to turn every bad thing around for your good. It trusts that He’s able to bring such blessings. Anything outside of this is an obstacle for the both of you.

It’s also important to let go of the offense, not only to forgive, but also to let go of regretting the events themselves. It’s important not only because you can’t change it, but also because if you dwell on the loss, you deny the good that God can bring out of it. You’re not in a position to receive the turning of the matter. You’re not in a position to receive the blessing, the redeeming of the time. You’re not positioned to receive recompense seven times what was stolen. You’re not looking out for the anointing to break yokes off of the offender that propels them into their destinies. You can’t love people because you’re stuck looking for justice. You’re not seeking healing yourself.
God’s vengeance will never be about taking delight in retribution, only in justice. It is not offended and seeking its own. It will always seek that which was at the heart of what really hurt us to begin with: that we were ignored. Our feelings, our wellbeing, and our consideration were all ignored in what was done to us. God’s grace abounds to bring people to the understanding of what was really done. Many people simply don’t realize. They don’t see clearly. After all, every man is righteous in his own eyes (). God’s grace does not condemn, but seeks to bring change without offense. There may be consequences for actions and violations, but 

Acts 8:23
For I see that you are poisoned by bitterness and bound by iniquity.

Notice that one of these precedes the other. Bitterness that we allow to take root creates the ideal conditions for iniquity to take hold.

The enemy is always trying to bring offense. He sets people us because he knows exactly what will cut deeply. The offenders are not seeing clearly what it will do to you. They’re blinded by their own offense, fear, or lack of faith. The enemy plays off of the hurts and traumas they’ve suffered so that he can blind them to ours. He hates us both. Don’t give him the satisfaction.
We need to desire for the blessings of God to overtake people. This has nothing to do with condoning sin and everything to do with seeing God’s plans and purposes for someone being fulfilled. This fulfillment entails a righting of wrongs, a clarity and clarifying of how God sees things, which will cleans the intents of the heart. It can bring repentance if it is warranted. understanding of God’s purposes and righteousness being manifested in someone’s life. Whenever there’s offense, there’s been a setup, sabotage, and a trap. The one who saw the evil in the situation was the devil, not the offender. That’s why so many times people don’t even see that they did anything wrong. They certainly didn’t start out wanting it to be personal. 4
There is a very distinct difference between forgiveness of sins and redemption from consequence. God is not mocked; whatever a man sows so shall he also reap. We have a harvest ripening based on every word and action. Each person does. Being born again does not absolve us from this. We have been given the power to overcome the tendency towards sin, not the freedom to continue in it. That’s not freedom, anyway. The Bible clearly equates sin with bondage and slavery. 
We forgive people, absolving them of judgment, because we have full confidence that God has our backs. He sees every little thing and nothing gets overlooked. Forgiving puts us in a frame of operating in God’s love so that we can freely receive, letting God put things right, restoring to us what was stolen, healing us. 
We aren’t just told to let things go. We’re told to love our enemies. If we love them, we’ll want the best for them. We’ll want good things to happen to them. It is us that breaks the cycle of an eye for an eye. It’s the leverage the enemy wants to use to steal, kill and destroy.
In reality, forgiving and letting go of bitterness is likely the hardest thing we have to do. We find safety in holding onto the offense because that where we hold onto control of our destinies. It never works. It’s where we maintain an identity of a victim. It’s not meant for us, though. We’ve been made overcomers for a reason. It’s a place of total surrender to let go of the bitterness, because then we let go of the control to make our lives what we want of it. It’s alright. God can be trusted to make our lives beautiful. Letting go is what frees Him up to do so. There must be that exchange. As long as you hold onto the bitterness and offense, you’re retaining control of your life. 
Our offenses against others create judgments, which derail us from our destinies. They are open portals for the enemy to undermine us. When we forgive others, they are forgiven in heaven. Then judgment becomes correction. God will lovingly correct us, but that should be the extent of the outcome we should desire. 
None of these things has to do with keeping ourselves open to others who have hurt us, especially if they are not repentant. Especially if they have hurt us repeatedly. Nobody is entitled to restored relationship and no one is immune to a modified relationship. It just can’t be that we use offense to be an excuse for breaking relationship as a punishment. But broken relationship doesn’t automatically mean punishment. Often it’s a boundary. God hasn’t called us to be a doormat. It is not selfish to protect ourselves. It’s not fleshly to disconnect from people, especially those that might expect it in order to keep being able to do what they’ve always done. The word says that we are to show the fruits of repentance. If someone is not showing a commitment, not just a desire, to change, then we can distance ourselves. But we must have God’s direction on how to navigate each and every relationship. 
Forgiveness is a spiritual revelation that you are choosing to flow in line with God’s Spirit. You are releasing the people involved to God’s hand, not excusing them. In doing so, you are choosing to love them, to want the best for them, but it will include God dealing with them appropriately. And God does not miss one iota of anything. 
We’re often told about what bitterness will do to us. People are told that forgiveness is for them rather than the person that offended us. We’re told to not let others live rent free in our minds. It’s true, but it’s only a part of it. It’s so much more than that. And we need all of it in order to really do any of it.
It can be so hard to let go because we’re afraid that God will forget as well. We’re afraid the offense to our being will be overlooked, that the pain will have been in vain. The only thing that is in vain is the pain itself that continues. God does forgive, but in that forgiveness is an acknowledgment of the offense. He doesn’t miss anything, however small. And He may let go of the judgment, but He will not call it something other than what it was. He won’t excuse it because He is just. He will make sure that somehow, some way the truth of the matter is known. Whether through conviction or simply revelation, even discipline, He will deal with the matter. This leaves us free to let it go because we can trust Him with it. Yes, it matters. And He brings His love to the situation, to heal, not to excuse. 
When people offend, when they sin against someone else, it creates an open door for the enemy to do damage in their lives. When we forgive, we take that power away from the devil and only God’s loving instruction is what brings change, but it’s the change that is good for everyone. It brings the revelation of truth so that people can understand how their actions have caused pain. They can understand how and why things should have been different, and it’s done without condemnation. It’s the kind of correction that builds up rather than tears down. His loving instruction corrects, draws people up higher, just like how He deals with us: without condemnation. 
In reality, the enemy is always seeking to set us up, often through offense and hurt, in order to cause division, but it’s more than that. If we sin against one another, it not only causes a divide, but the sins are open doors for  him to operate and bring destruction in our own lives. When others sin against us, it is actually the enemy trying to destroy us both. 
This is why Jesus said that when we forgive others, it is forgiven in heaven. It has to do with the curse brought about by the sin. God does not ignore sin, even when we are His child and are redeemed. Sin opens doors for the enemy to bring destruction in many forms into someone’s life. He’s always looking to trap people into sinning and it’s compounded when others are offended against them. God is still there to correct, but it is always done in love. Even when it results in unwanted consequences, it has been decided based in love and that all other options had been exhausted. 
Forgiveness usually isn’t so difficult because of what we’ve lost. What tends to gut us more than anything is that someone did something that goes against our person. They disregarded who we were, what was important to us, what was in our best interest. They disregarded our hearts. They disregarded our humanity. They certainly disregarded who God sees in us. What they did was the opposite of love.
Ultimately, when we decide to forgive, it is an act of love. Peter illustrated this when he said, “Above all things have intense and unfailing love for one another, for love covers a multitude of sins [forgives and disregards the offenses of others]. (I Peter 4:8 AMPC).
Offense is all a set-up by the enemy. It’s all a ruse to get people to be divided and to run contrary to what God is doing. That’s why the Bible says we fight not against flesh and blood, but against powers and principalities and rulers of darkness in heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12). 
The trouble with bitterness is that it often masquerades as wisdom as we push it down into our subconscious. We keep the offense on a shelf to remind us of what not to get ourselves entangled with in the future. The tricky part is that there really is wisdom in that, but bitterness is a chameleon. It is a blanket of barnacles on the underbelly of a well-meaning ship navigating through the rough waters of life. 
The lie the enemy tells us is that God misses things, that He lets things slide as a package deal with forgiveness. What letting go provides is God blessing them with the knowledge and revelation of what they’ve done. He always draws people to a closer relationship with Him so that they can be blessed, but with it comes knowledge, awareness, and conviction. We may not see the results of it, but it’s the goodness of God that leads to repentance. Letting go of bitterness opens the door for God to deal with them in a way that is beneficial to all. It opens the door for the person to be brought forward in their destiny, in their calling. It breaks strongholds the enemy constructs to divide and conquer. 
Staying angry at someone is a form of punishment. It’s exacting revenge on someone. That doesn’t mean you have to stay in someone’s life, particularly if they are not repentant. 
When we take offense, when we decide that we can’t let it go, it is the same as saying that God won’t fix things, that He won’t bless us, that His hand is waxed short over our lives. It is not recognizing our relationship with Him. Being angry and staying angry at someone means we don’t trust God to rectify the situation. Without realizing it, this is how we exact revenge because we’re punishing people for not seeing what we see about the situation. We’re not trusting and resting in the fact that absolutely nothing escapes God’s notice and that He actually cares about every tiny thing. It gets tricky because neither are we to ignore wrongs against us that will communicate that we accept their behavior and, therefore, invite it in the future. There’s a fine line there. Offense damages a connection and if others don’t deal with the damage, it can create distance. There are people whom we find ourselves having only a superficial relationship with. Their past actions and lack of repentance can and do inform our decisions of what we trust them with in the future. Just because we’re called to forgive seventy times seven times, doesn’t mean we are to purposely put ourselves in the position to need to forgive that many times. We just have to continue to lay the situation before God as often as necessary so we’re not hiding bitterness behind those boundaries.
One way to think about it is that we’re not taking away the action. We’re taking away the offense of the action.
The enemy had a very specific message in the offense he managed against us. It was meant to offend out being in every way possible, even if the person who offended us was not privy to it at all. They may not have even seen their actions as being offensive in the first place. 
It’s a dynamic of the spiritual realm. The Spirit does not flow in unforgiveness. It hinders the  advancement of the Kingdom of God. It blocks our influence and authority in the earth.
It can be so hard to let go of offenses, not because we don’t want to let go, not because we’re being stubborn or obstinate, but because it was so personal. It’s that way by design. 
When we hang onto the anger and offense, we’re holding onto the responsibility to fix your circumstances, the job of righting wrongs. When we forgive, we’re making the space for God to take over, to bless your life, and to correct everyone involved in what hurt you.
It’s not that the offense doesn’t inform your future. It’s that it no longer informs your present. 
Forgiveness is not only an act of faith that God will bless your life and has control of your story, but it’s an act of faith that He sees what happened did to your heart. He considers the pain you went through and knows how to administer justice that is right for all. 
Jesus said that what we forgive on earth will be forgiven in heaven. This makes forgiveness a spiritual weapon. Sin brings curses. It’s an open door for the enemy to move in one’s life. Forgiveness breaks that off, freeing the person to move in their destiny, perhaps even deterring the offense that might make the offender not seek to right things themselves.
When we hang onto the bitterness and offense, we’re keeping control of the situation. We’re seeking to punish with our begrudging demeanor. As long as we hang onto it, God cannot take care of it Himself. We have to not excuse it, but relinquish it. 
The offenses people do against us are really a setup and a trick of the enemy. He tricks people into acting in ways outside of love so that he can create wedges between people. If he can wedge his way in, it causes division and with division we lose spiritual momentum. We lose power and spiritual sensitivity. We have to know who the real enemy is and recognize him so that he doesn’t have that foothold in our lives, thwarting our destinies, legacies, and blessings God wants for us.
Strive for a vision for them for a blessed life. This is love. We have to see the offender as someone that was used of the enemy to bring division and destruction. We tend to want people to pay for what they’ve done wrong, but the enemy is always out to try to steal, kill, and destroy. We can’t align ourselves with him.
Forgiving others can even be cathartic. It delineates what happened. It distinguishes what was offensive as offensive and it distinguishes the offender as no longer such, because they’re also the creation and beloved of God. We’re able to live the truth of 1 John 4:20 (AMPC):
If anyone says, I love God, and hates (detests, abominates) his brother [[a]in Christ], he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, Whom he has not seen.
It not only releases the forgiver from bitterness, but also spiritual entanglements. It releases the forgiver from the curses of their own shortcomings.
Ultimately, when we are unwilling to let go of the hurts, it’s because we’re looking at our lives as orphans, because we’re not seeing how God can take control and make things right. We’re not trusting Him because we’re not abiding in His love. But perfect love casts out fear and he who fears has not been made perfect in love. 1 John 4:18
We forgive out of love, but also as an act of love. 
All of this can only truly come by the Spirit of God. As always, He is the true hero. He’s the enabler of righteousness who gives us the vision and understanding of the battle so that we all can walk free.

There is a showdown with many becoming increasingly obstinate in their stances. There are various opinions on what exactly is dividing us, but no one seems to be advocating for the idea that everything is copacetic with a unifying, assentive energy. 
At times like these, it’s so easy to feel like the end of the world could be in our purview. We do not feel fine. As believers, we know a great tribulation will come upon the earth. Jesus said it’s impossible that offenses should not come, but woe to those through whom they come (Luke 17:1). Offense is an enticement to sin. The types of offenses He was talking about are those that lead to direct sin, such as seduction, drug use, etc. It can be traumas we inflict on children that cause them to feel the need to run away from God and towards the darkness that hurt them. But we can be offended in less direct ways as well. Sometimes we get offended when we see godly men and women knowingly and regularly commit sin and we are disillusioned. We wonder how people who seemed to know the truth, seemed to love God, could so wantonly do what flies in the face of what they claim. It can cause some people who were under their leadership to question their own salvation experience, particularly when we may not be feeling God’s presence at that moment. The devil is always there, ready to pounce at any and every opportunity to plant those seeds of doubt through confusion. He doesn’t mind waiting for them to grow. In fact, if they can grow undetected the better. 
Sometimes, however, we can become offended by God. We know He’s not our own personal Santa Claus, yet sometimes we’re particularly disillusioned by how some things turn out. It hits us in our innermost being and we’re face-to-face with the knowledge that God let it happen to us. It belies the faith that we have that God loves us so intimately and cares about every little thing concerning us. We can think it’ll never happen to us, but in our vulnerability and desperation, that confusion and hurt can overcome us. Trite saying from others just make it worse.
And yet, sometimes it’s because of what happens on a grand scale. Events such as the Holocaust has caused many to wonder how He could have let something so unspeakably egregious happen. It can make the wicked appear mighty. This is certainly true of the Egyptians. The Hebrews had been enslaved for 400 years. It was so normal to them they probably never expected to be delivered, at least in their lifetimes. Maybe they thought Egypt was too powerful for God to deliver them. This would only be amplified when Moses came along, followed by plagues, only for matters to get worse. Yet, it all changed in a day. What seemed impossible, what seemed like what would completely finish them off, had the rug pulled out from under it overnight. Perspective is so unreliable.

Sometimes, the most faith-filled thing you can do is just to tell God, “I’m not giving up.” 

“In this hour, I do not believe that any darkness will endure.”
― J.R.R. Tolkien, The Return of the King
